goal: Keep csv-report reliable and maintainable for the analyst who runs it as a single script, while deciding how its CSV processing should be implemented.
question: Should csv-report keep its standard-library-only CSV processing, or add an external data-handling dependency?
known_constraints: The tool must keep running as a single script on the analyst's laptop.
Weekly file sizes are unmeasured and vary a lot between weeks.
The repository currently has no dependency manifest, test suite, or CI.
The currently required output is a row count for the weekly export.

environment.deployment: Single script run manually on an analyst's laptop
environment.dependency_manifest: none (no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, setup.py, or lockfile)

evidence: process.py is 12 lines: it opens 'export.csv', wraps it in csv.reader, and prints 'rows: N' where N comes from sum(1 for _ in rows).
process.py's docstring states: 'Turn the weekly CSV export into a summary report (stdlib only today).' — the stdlib-only state is explicit and recent.

README.md states: 'An internal tool that turns the weekly CSV export into a summary report. It runs as a single script on the analyst's laptop. Nobody has measured how large the weekly files get; sizes vary a lot between weeks.'
The repository contains exactly README.md and process.py — no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, setup.py, lockfile, tests, or CI configuration — and it is not a git repository.
csv.reader is a lazy iterator; the current summarizer consumes it with a generator expression, so the existing row count already uses memory proportional to one row rather than to file size.
No sample export.csv exists in the repository, so actual weekly file sizes cannot be measured from the repo itself.
Python's csv module ships with the interpreter, is documented, and is backed by the C-accelerated _csv implementation; no third-party package is required for RFC 4180-style CSV parsing.

alternatives.name: Keep standard-library CSV processing
alternatives.description: Continue using only Python's built-in csv module to read and summarize the weekly export, with no new third-party dependencies.
advantages: No install, pinning, or environment-management burden on the analyst's laptop
The existing 12-line implementation already satisfies the current requirement (row counting) and streams rows lazily
csv module behavior for quoting, embedded newlines, and dialects is documented in the standard library
disadvantages: Any future aggregation beyond counting (grouping, joins, statistics) must be hand-written
Performance on very large files is unverified because weekly file sizes have never been measured
assumptions: The tool's job stays close to summarizing a single weekly CSV export
Standard-library csv performance is adequate for the actual file sizes once they are measured

alternatives.name: Add a data-handling dependency
alternatives.description: Add a third-party data-handling library such as pandas or polars and move CSV loading and summarization onto it.
advantages: Richer aggregation, filtering, and grouping are available without custom code
Columnar or vectorized implementations can be fast on very large files
Common CSV parsing edge cases are handled and tested by a widely used library
disadvantages: Introduces install and version-pinning burden into a single-script laptop tool that currently has no dependency manifest, tests, or CI
Larger download and environment footprint for a job that is currently one row count
Rewrites working 12-line code and adds a library API and upgrade path to maintain
assumptions: The analyst can install and upgrade third-party packages on the laptop where the tool runs
Future analysis needs will justify the dependency weight

alternatives.name: Keep stdlib now, define a measurable trigger to revisit
alternatives.description: Keep the standard-library-only implementation and record an explicit measurable trigger — such as a measured weekly file size, a new aggregation requirement, or observed slowness — at which the dependency decision is reopened.
advantages: Avoids dependency weight today while the requirement is a single row count
Replaces the unmeasured-size unknown with a concrete decision rule, which directly addresses the README's admission that file sizes were never measured
Requires no code changes now, so existing behavior is untouched
disadvantages: Defers rather than resolves future capability needs; a trigger must be written down and someone must act on it
If file sizes grow abruptly, the tool gains nothing from optimized libraries until the trigger is noticed
assumptions: A trigger can be written down and observed in normal use of the tool
Row counting with the standard library remains adequate until a trigger fires

criteria.name: Fit to the current requirement
rubric: Fails to produce the required weekly row count
Produces the row count but with rework or risk to existing behavior
Produces the row count with documented CSV edge-case handling and no rework of working code

criteria.name: Operational footprint on the analyst's laptop
rubric: Adds a large dependency tree that must be installed and pinned on a machine with no manifest, tests, or CI
Adds a small, contained third-party dependency
Adds no new installation or pinning burden

criteria.name: Resilience to unmeasured, highly variable file sizes
rubric: Loads whole files into memory or is untested at large sizes with no plan to find out
Streams or scales to large files but leaves the size unknown and unmanaged
Streams or scales to large files and turns the unknown size into something measured or explicitly watched

criteria.name: Capability if analysis needs grow
rubric: New aggregations require hand-writing custom logic
Common aggregations, grouping, and filtering are available out of the box

criteria.name: Maintainability and reviewability
rubric: Adds moving parts (dependency versions, upgrades) to an unmanaged single script
Keeps the change surface small and reviewable with documented standard-library behavior
